title: the Panchadashi (selections)
tomorrow: a father weeps for a son who's alive and well. why?

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana closed the Brahma Sutras: know the one clay, and every pot is known. Today, a new book that teaches the same view in plain verses, starting with your ears.

The morning after a loud night: the music's gone, the room is quiet, and the ears still hum. A car passes. A bird calls. Someone laughs in the next room. Each sound is different, and each one fades. The Panchadashi opens on something that ordinary. The sounds, the sights, the touches of a waking day keep changing. So, one question today. When every sound in the room changes, does anything stay?
screen: `THE MORNING AFTER THE MUSIC.` → `A CAR. A BIRD. A LAUGH.` → `DOES ANYTHING STAY?`

segments.voice: The Panchadashi is a book of verses on Advaita Vedanta, and tradition credits it to Vidyaranya, a teacher of Shankara's line. Its answer: yes. In waking, objects differ: sound, touch, form, taste, smell. But the knowing of them isn't split up among them. Hearing the car and hearing the bird, the knowing is one. In a dream the objects change again, and still the knowing is the same. Then deep sleep, where nothing is seen. Yet on waking a person says, I slept and knew nothing. Who was there to know the nothing? From this the book makes its bold claim. This awareness neither rises nor sets. It shines by its own light. A neighbor tradition sings something close. A psalm in the Hebrew Bible, in the King James Version, looks at the earth and heavens and says: "as a vesture shalt thou change them, and they shall be changed: But thou art the same, and thy years shall have no end." Here's what they share: everything seen changes, and something does not. And the honest difference. The psalm says it to God, a thou the singer turns to and trusts. The Panchadashi says the unchanging is awareness itself, a person's own self. Two old voices, both refusing to let the changing be the whole story.
screen: `THE SOUNDS DIFFER; THE KNOWING DOESN'T.` · `WAKING, DREAM, DEEP SLEEP.` · `THE PSALM: THOU ART THE SAME.` · `SAID TO GOD, OR FOUND AS THE SELF.` · then, large: `IT NEITHER RISES NOR SETS.`

segments.voice: Listen for the sounds around you, one at a time: a hum, a car, a voice, your own breath. Let each one arrive and fade without following it. Then, between sounds, notice the hearing itself, there before the next one comes, still there after it goes.
The Panchadashi: a book of Advaita verses that opens with the senses. Sounds change; the knowing of them stays one.
Your line: the Panchadashi, selections, where the knowing neither rises nor sets. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, the Panchadashi is studied with a teacher as an introduction to the tradition's view of the self, often beginning with this opening on waking, dream and deep sleep. Psalm 102 is part of the Hebrew Bible, read by Jews and Christians.

fork.setup: you wake up and say: I slept well and knew nothing at all. what does the Panchadashi hear in that sentence?
options: someone was there to know the nothing: awareness didn't switch off.
the mind was simply gone, and there's nothing more to it.
a dream you've forgotten, so nothing can be learned.
fork.reveal: The verses ask who was there to know the nothing. So the knowing was there through waking, dream and deep sleep, neither rising nor setting.

original.note: Sanskrit Panchadashi, the name of this book of Advaita verses credited by tradition to Vidyaranya.

what a scholar hears: Panchadashi 1.3–7 (Tattva-viveka), with self-luminous awareness that neither rises nor sets; read beside Psalm 102:26–27.

chat.says: Sam's grandma came!! she said our bhajan reminded her of a psalm: 'thou art the same.' same idea?
options: close, not identical: both hold something unchanging; the psalm says it to God.
exactly the same idea, just in another language with different words.

chat.meaning: Both say something stays while everything changes. The psalm addresses God as unchanging; the Panchadashi finds the unchanging as awareness, the self.
